item.title: Boston Transit Quality Maps
item.description:
Now that I can delegate problems to AI, I've been going back over some of my old projects to do them better and more in depth. Friday this was my rent map, earlier it was my mixer, rhythm stage setup, bass whistle, and clipboard normalizer. Today I'm picking back up my Boston transit quality map:

(interactive version)

In 2010 I made a map, which I'd wanted for a while, showing how well you can get around on transit. Each point represented the average travel time to every other point. Iterating on it with Claude, this version improves it in a bunch of ways:

  • Originally I built this by post-processing a set of maps Dan Tillberg made; now it routes directly from MBTA GTFS data.

  • OpenStreetMap for walking times, instead of (guessing; I don't have Tillberg's source code) straight-line distance.

  • For simplicity, the original map treated every destination as equally valuable. Aside from being unrealistic, this also unfairly advantaged the center of the map. The new one can weight by jobs or residents (both from the Census).

  • It no longer estimates over water or other inaccessible areas.

  • It builds maps annually going back to 2009, and lets you explore the ways areas have gotten better or worse transit over time. (interactive history page)

Overall, things have gotten substantially slower. Here's 2009 vs 2026, with areas that got slower in orange, and the areas that got faster are in purple:

Let's start with the four bright spots. The biggest improvement is Assembly Square, which got an infill station on the Orange Line in 2014. Here's the year-over-year comparison, showing a ~6min improvement in an area that now has 1.6k residents and 10k jobs:

The other three spots are good, but a smaller impact:

  • Chelsea gained the SL3, which improved service north of the Chelsea St Bridge. This covers ~500 residents and ~1.1k jobs.

  • The tiny suburban Endicott Station in Dedham got better morning inbound train timing. This covers ~900 residents and very few jobs.

  • The Stone Zoo gained service from route 132. This covers no (human) residents and the census seems not to count the zoo jobs, but this illustrates that commutes aren't everything. People also go to the zoo.

These are the only bright spots in an overall very sad picture. Whether we look by residents or jobs, 99% have slower commutes than in 2009. This is mostly driven by slower buses:

You can see a brief speed up during COVID, when traffic was lower, though overall I'd rather have slower buses and no pandemic.

This also means the ~same number of bus-hours only complete 23% fewer trips:

And so it mostly impacts residents who are farther out, who are more reliant on buses:

This means fewer homes are good places to live for a public transit commute, and fewer jobs are well-served by transit. If we count a home as being in the "transit area" if you can reach at least 10% of jobs within 45 minutes, and vice versa, you can see both "transit areas" shrank:

The big caveat here is that we don't actually know how fast things moved, just how fast they were scheduled to move. If 2026 schedules have more padding, once you get on your bus you might be arriving sooner than predicted. I had Claude look into whether this is a change in an approach to padding. The MBTA shares actual running time [1], in addition to the schedules I've been using for this post. We can see how both scheduled and actual performance have changed since the MBTA started releasing actuals in 2018-08:

Overall it looks like a change in actual speed, not in approaches to padding. Speeds increased during the pandemic, and then decreased again. The MBTA, not surprisingly, takes some time to turn observed performance into schedule changes. More interestingly, the MBTA sharply overestimated how quickly things would return to normal: as we got into Fall and Winter 2020, COVID got worse but the MBTA scheduled buses assuming pre-COVID levels of traffic, and only gradually corrected. Since then, both the schedule and the actual have been getting worse.

The small amount of bus lanes and transit signal priority buildout over this period has not been enough to counter the large increase in traffic. While more of those would probably help, I'd like to go farther and add congestion pricing. This has been moderately successful in NYC. Overall, though, making buses fast is just very hard. If I didn't expect AI was about to massively remake the world I'd be advocating for investing in more efficient and expanded subways.

Claude estimates it contributed 3% of words and 30% of ideas; it also built the new maps, processed the historical schedule and bus performance data, and made the charts, while I directed what to show and wrote the post.


[1] Downloads go back to 2020, but it looks like at one point it went back to 2018. I think maybe the MBTA portal only keeps the most recent 7y? To get the 2018 and 2019 data I had Claude download from TransitMatters. This isn't perfect: it's only 83 of the routes that TM tracks instead of the whole system, but it includes the busiest ones. Claude calibrated the TM subset against the full official data during the period where we have both, and used that to project back to cover 2018 and 2019. This is why the first 1.5y are a different color on the chart.

item.title: What us little people are doing about ASI risk
item.description:
Hi LW... just wanted to introduce myself and let you folks know you're not alone.  The non-professional cavalry is on the way as more and more of us lay people wake up to ASI x-risk.   My relevant experience is more in civil disobedience and mass communication than science or programming....so it's easy to feel underpowered and overwhelmed by the dangers your community has flagged.

 

But even little folk can play their part. What I have done is write some articles and try to promote the "unsung heroes of the singularity" via talk radio calls. Whenever practical, I call a list of shows and talk up the work of AI safety folk whose ideas seem most promising and thoughtful....Steve Byrnes, Nick Bostrom, Liron Shapira and probably some of you who are reading this. 

 

Most of the talk radio calls are un-linkable, but here is my article about Daniel Kokotajlo:

 

https://freekeene.com/2025/07/17/misaligned-superintelligence-will-it-delete-new-hampshire/

 

Thanks for what you're doing...most of it, anyway.  Looking forward to connecting with your community!
